research_text:
## Research brief — `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` / `UnsafeProtocol`

### 1. What `SSLContext` governs, and what the reported value refers to

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` is the JSSE engine class representing a secure-socket-protocol implementation. It acts as a factory for `SSLSocketFactory`, `SSLServerSocketFactory`, and `SSLEngine`, and holds state shared by objects created from it, including session state. Its `init` configuration supplies the key and trust managers used for authentication and key agreement. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

For the reported literal comparison, the relevant API event is the **protocol-name argument passed to `SSLContext.getInstance(...)`**, not a handshake result. The Java API defines that parameter as “the standard name of the requested protocol,” and `SSLContext.getProtocol()` returns the same name supplied to a `getInstance` call. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The distinction matters:

* A context/factory algorithm name is **not itself** the set of enabled endpoint protocols or the negotiated protocol.
* Oracle’s JSSE guide says that a context-created `SSLSocket`, `SSLServerSocket`, or `SSLEngine` has a set of **supported** protocols, while the endpoint’s enabled protocols are controlled separately, including by `setEnabledProtocols(String[])`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))
* The standard-name specification describes both `"SSL"` and `"TLS"` as broad algorithm names: `"SSL"` supports some SSL version and may support other SSL/TLS versions; `"TLS"` supports some TLS version and may support other SSL/TLS versions. Thus, neither name alone documents an actual negotiated version. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

Accordingly, the supplied detector message refers to a **literal/static-policy predicate on the `getInstance` argument**. It is not documentation that an SSL/TLS connection negotiated a particular protocol, nor a runtime conclusion about certificate validation, hostname verification, or an actual handshake.

### 2. Official API guidance, safe usage, and documented remediation

The current Java SE API requires Java-platform implementations to support `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3` as `SSLContext` protocols; it directs users to implementation release documentation for any additional protocol support. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The official documentation also establishes these usage points:

* `getInstance` selects a provider implementation for the requested protocol name; a provider-specific context can implement more than the requested protocol. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
* A newly created context is initialized through `init(KeyManager[], TrustManager[], SecureRandom)`. The API explicitly permits `null` key-manager or trust-manager arrays, in which case installed providers are searched; it also permits a `null` `SecureRandom`, in which case the default implementation is used. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
* For raw `SSLSocket` or `SSLEngine` use, the JSSE guide says to check peer credentials before sending data, and explains that endpoint identification can be performed during the handshake. It specifically identifies hostname matching as necessary for the peer identity check. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))
* For `SSLEngine`, the API recommends explicitly setting client or server mode because the default is provider-specific. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

**No official Java API source located labels `SSLContext.getInstance("SSL")` as an API error or gives a universal “replace it with X” remediation.** In fact, `"SSL"` is documented as a standard `SSLContext` algorithm name, and the JSSE guide presents `"TLS"` as a protocol-string example. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

For the **specific CrySL rule** supplied, however, its literal constraint accepts only `"TLSv1.2"` and `"TLSv1.3"`—not `"SSL"` and not `"TLS"`. That rule condition is a static-rule requirement, separate from the broader Java API contract. The API’s documented acceptance of `null` initialization arguments also does not establish satisfaction of CrySL’s separate `generatedKeyManagers`, `generatedTrustManagers`, and `randomized` predicates. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

### 3. Compatibility, formats, platform support, and documented migration information

**Persisted formats.** The examined `SSLContext` API and JSSE guide do not define a persisted application-data or `SSLContext` serialization format whose compatibility changes when the requested context algorithm name changes. They document in-memory/session state associated with a context and session reuse, but do not provide a persisted-format migration procedure for this API choice. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

**Wire protocol and negotiation.** The documentation distinguishes the requested context algorithm from endpoint configuration and handshake negotiation. TLS 1.3 uses the `supported_versions` extension for version negotiation and retains a legacy TLS 1.2 value in the ClientHello version field. That is a TLS wire-format behavior, not evidence that a particular `getInstance` string will negotiate a particular version. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

**TLS 1.3 compatibility.** Oracle documents that TLS 1.3 is not directly compatible with prior TLS versions, even though it can operate in a backward-compatibility mode. Documented transition concerns include half-close versus duplex-close behavior, certificate signature restrictions including lack of DSA support, changed cipher-suite sets, and changed session-resumption/key-update behavior. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

**Platform-version support.**

* The current Java SE 27 API requires `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
* Oracle documented TLS 1.2 support in the SunJSSE provider beginning with Java SE 7. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/technotes/guides/security/enhancements-7.html))
* Oracle documented TLS 1.3 in JDK 11, enabled by default there. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/24/migrate/security-updates.html))
* Oracle also documented TLS 1.3 support in JDK 8 beginning with **8u261**. In that release, TLS 1.3 was disabled by default for client endpoints of default `"SSL"` or `"TLS"` contexts, while the release notes listed endpoint and system-property mechanisms for enabling it. ([oracle.com](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/8u261-relnotes.html))

**Documented migration path.** The sources document mechanisms for controlling enabled protocols at the socket/engine/`SSLParameters` level and, for SunJSSE, relevant client/server system properties. They do **not** provide a universal migration guarantee for changing an application’s `SSLContext.getInstance` string. The choice depends on the deployed JDK/provider, protocol configuration at endpoints, peer support, cipher suites, certificates, and application behavior that depends on TLS 1.2 versus TLS 1.3 handshake or closure semantics. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

### 4. Exact CrySL matching rule in the cited source

**Primary rule source:**  
`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl`

The source scopes the specification to this exact type:

> `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`

It therefore does **not** state a generic, name-only rule that applies to arbitrary methods named `getInstance`, `init`, `createSSLEngine`, or `getDefault`. **No: based on the declared `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` scope, this source does not match a method merely because it shares one of those names on another API type.** The source has no wildcard or alternate receiver type. It also does not independently describe the CrySL engine’s compiler/resolution mechanics beyond that declared specification scope. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

The source’s matching clauses are, verbatim:

```text
SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext

FORBIDDEN
	getDefault() => Get;

EVENTS
	g1: getInstance(protocol);
	g2: getInstance(protocol, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	i1: init(km, tm, random);
	Init := i1;

	se1: eng = createSSLEngine();
	se2: eng = createSSLEngine(_,_);
	Engine := se1 | se2;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

The parameter-list effects stated by that source are:

| Event | Method pattern in source | Parameter constraint stated by source |
|---|---|---|
| `Get` | `getInstance(protocol)` | One argument, captured as `protocol`. |
| `Get` | `getInstance(protocol, _)` | Two arguments; first captured as `protocol`; second is `_`, with no further source-level constraint. |
| `Init` | `init(km, tm, random)` | Three arguments captured as declared objects: `KeyManager[]`, `TrustManager[]`, and `SecureRandom`. |
| `Engine` | `eng = createSSLEngine()` | Zero arguments; result captured as `SSLEngine eng`. |
| `Engine` | `eng = createSSLEngine(_,_)` | Two arguments represented by unconstrained `_` placeholders; result captured as `eng`. |
| Forbidden | `getDefault()` | No arguments; forbidden and mapped to `Get`. |

The subsequent condition and trace requirements are, verbatim:

```text
ORDER
	Get, Init, Engine?
CONSTRAINTS
	protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"};

REQUIRES
	generatedKeyManagers[km];
	generatedTrustManagers[tm];
	randomized[random];
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

Thus, the source evaluates:

1. the `Get → Init → optional Engine` order;
2. the exact `protocol` membership condition `{"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"}`;
3. the three `Init`-argument predicates; and
4. the independent prohibition of `getDefault()`.

**Source discrepancy requiring confirmation:** the supplied detector presentation says it expects `TLSV1.2,TLSV1.3,TLS`, whereas the cited raw CrySL source contains only exact literals `"TLSv1.2"` and `"TLSv1.3"`—with lowercase `v` and no `"TLS"` alternative. The source does not explain that discrepancy or any diagnostic label such as “unknown.” Resolving it requires the detector version, compiled rule artifact, and original diagnostic metadata; it cannot be determined from this CrySL source alone.
